Content:
Loosely speaking, a rational equation is an equation containing rational expressions.

Content:
When a rational equation contains only one fractional term, like

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{2}{x} = 1 ,]

Content:
we can multiply both sides of the equation by the denominator to remove the fraction. This leaves us with a linear equation, which we can then solve using the addition and multiplication principles.

Content:
Before we proceed, we note that [MATH: x=0] cannot be a solution. This is because if [MATH: x=0] then the rational term would be [MATH: \dfrac{2}{0},] which is undefined because it has a zero denominator.

Content:
To solve the equation, we multiply both sides by the denominator [MATH: {\color{blue} x}] to get rid of the fraction:
[MATH: (2)/(x)|= 1; x ⋅ (2)/(x)|= x ⋅ 1; x ⋅ (2)/(x)|= x ⋅ 1; 2|= x.]

Content:
Since [MATH: x=2] is different from [MATH: x=0], we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is [MATH: x=2.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that [MATH: x=2] cannot be a solution. This is because if [MATH: x=2,] then the rational term would be [MATH: \dfrac{1}{0},] which is undefined because it has a zero denominator.

To solve the equation, we first multiply both sides by the denominator [MATH: (x-2)] to get rid of the fraction:

[MATH: (1)/(x − 2)|= 5; (x − 2) ⋅ (1)/(x − 2)|= (x − 2) ⋅ 5; (x − 2) ⋅ (1)/(x − 2)|= 5x − 10; 1|= 5x − 10]

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

[MATH: 1|= 5x − 10; 1 + 10|= 5x − 10 + 10; 11|= 5x; (11)/(5)|= (5x)/(5); (11)/(5)|= x]

Since [MATH: x=\dfrac{11}{5}] is different from [MATH: x=2], we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is [MATH: x=\dfrac{11}{5}.]

items.title: Equations Containing Variables in the Numerator and Denominator

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that [MATH: x=-1] cannot be a solution since division by [MATH: 0] is undefined.

To solve the equation, we first multiply both sides by the denominator [MATH: (x+1)] to get rid of the fraction:

[MATH: (3x)/(x + 1)|= 2; (x + 1) ⋅ (3x)/(x + 1)|= (x + 1) ⋅ 2; (x + 1) ⋅ (3x)/(x + 1)|= 2x + 2; 3x|= 2x + 2]

Then, we apply the addition principle:

[MATH: 3x|= 2x + 2; 3x − 2x|= 2x + 2 − 2x; x|= 2]

Since [MATH: x = 2] is different from [MATH: x=-1], we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is [MATH: x=2.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that the denominator [MATH: 2x+1] cannot be zero, since division by [MATH: 0] is undefined. Therefore we cannot have [MATH: 2x+1=0,] which means [MATH: x=-\dfrac{1}{2}] cannot be a solution.

To solve the equation, we first multiply both sides by the denominator [MATH: (2x+1)] to get rid of the fraction:

[MATH: (1)/(2x + 1)|= 2; (2x + 1) ⋅ (1)/(2x + 1)|= (2x + 1) ⋅ 2; (2x + 1) ⋅ (1)/(2x + 1)|= 4x + 2; 1|= 4x + 2]

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

[MATH: 1|= 4x + 2; 1 − 2|= 4x + 2 − 2; − 1|= 4x; (− 1)/(4)|= (4x)/(4); − (1)/(4)|= x]

Since [MATH: x = -\dfrac{1}{4}] is different from [MATH: x=-\dfrac{1}{2}], we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is [MATH: x=-\dfrac{1}{4}.]
